title: Goat's milk and honey cold-process soap
subtitle: A mild, creamy bar with a gentle lather
excerpt: A cold-process bar made with olive, coconut, and castor oils, using frozen goat's milk as the lye liquid and raw honey stirred in at trace. The milk proteins keep the bar mild and conditioning; the honey adds a faint sweetness to the lather. Makes seven bars; cure four to six weeks.
sourceNotes: Lye calculations using SoapCalc v3.0 with goat's milk as 100% of water weight. Olive oil SAP 0.134, coconut oil SAP 0.190, castor oil SAP 0.128 (NaOH per gram of oil). 5% superfat. Total oil weight 500 g. Honey addition: 1 tsp per 500 g oils at trace, as documented in Anne Bramson, Soap: Making It, Enjoying It (1972) and confirmed by the Handcrafted Soap & Cosmetic Guild technical notes.

recipe.batchNotes: Run any weight change through a lye calculator before making. Goat's milk batches are best kept at 500 g to 1 kg; above that the milk sugar acceleration is harder to manage.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Cure fully before gifting or using: four weeks minimum, six preferred. A well-cured bar is harder and the lather is fuller.
recipe.shelfLifeNotes: Stores two years or more in a cool dark cupboard once fully cured. Honey increases the risk of discolouration (the bar darkens to golden-tan, normal, not spoilage). Discard if orange patches of rancid oil (DOS) appear or the bar smells sharp and paint-like.

glossaryTerms.definition: The chemical reaction between fat and sodium hydroxide that produces soap and glycerine. Each oil has a SAP value, the grams of lye needed to fully saponify one gram of that oil.
The percentage of fat left unreacted in the finished bar, typically 5 to 8%. The unsaponified oil stays in the bar as a conditioning reserve.

The point at which soap batter thickens so that a drizzle on the surface briefly holds its shape before sinking back. The signal that oils and lye solution have emulsified and the batter is ready to pour.

projectSchedule.title: Unmould and cut
projectSchedule.body: Turn out the loaf. The bar will be darker than a water-based soap, honey and milk sugars stain it golden-tan, which is normal. Wear gloves: the bar is still caustic at this point. Cut into bars with a wire cutter or sharp knife and set on a rack.

projectSchedule.title: Four-week check
projectSchedule.body: The bars should be firm and dry to the touch. The lather should be stable and creamy. Safe to use from here, though the bar will improve further over another two weeks.

projectSchedule.title: Six-week cure complete
projectSchedule.body: A six-week goat's milk bar is firm, with a full creamy lather. The honey scent is faint and clean. Ready to use or gift.

content.text: Goat's milk and honey soap is a cold-process bar made with olive, coconut, and castor oils, with frozen goat's milk replacing the water in the lye solution and a teaspoon of raw honey stirred in at
. The milk proteins make the bar mild and conditioning; the honey adds a faint sweetness to the lather and helps retain moisture in the skin.
. Makes seven bars; cure for four to six weeks before use
Wear protective gloves and goggles before handling lye. Freeze the goat's milk the day before, adding lye to frozen milk slows the temperature rise and reduces scorching of the milk sugars.

items.prepNote: 30% of oil weight; melt gently; provides lather and hardness
10% of oil weight; stabilises and boosts lather
NaOH at 99% purity; calculated for 5% superfat on this oil blend
33% of oil weight; freeze in an ice-cube tray the day before
~1 tsp; stirred in at light trace

content.text: Work in a ventilated space wearing protective gloves and goggles. Place the frozen goat's milk cubes in the HDPE lye pitcher. Weigh the sodium hydroxide into a separate dry container. Add the lye to the frozen milk in a thin stream while stirring constantly. The milk will thaw and the solution will heat, keep stirring until all the lye dissolves. The solution may turn yellow or orange from the milk sugars; this is normal. Set aside to cool to 38 to 42°C.
Melt the coconut oil over a low heat. Combine with the olive and castor oils in a stainless-steel or heatproof bowl. Cool to 38 to 42°C, within a few degrees of the lye solution.

Pour the lye solution into the oils in a thin stream, stirring as you go. Use the stick blender in short 10-second bursts, alternating with hand-stirring. Milk-based batches can accelerate faster than water batches; work efficiently once blending starts. When the batter reaches a light
, the consistency of thin custard, stir in the honey quickly and blend for a few more seconds.

Pour immediately into the silicone loaf mould. Smooth the top with a spatula. Unlike water-based batches, do not insulate a milk soap, excess heat darkens the sugars and can cause overheating. Leave uncovered in a cool room for 24 to 48 hours.

After 48 hours check the soap: if it's firm enough to handle without deforming, turn it out. Wear gloves, still caustic at this stage. Cut into bars and arrange on a rack with space between them. Cure in a cool, dry space out of direct sunlight for four to six weeks.

At two weeks the bars are pale golden-tan and firm enough to turn. At four weeks the lather is full and creamy and the bar is safe to use. At six weeks the bar is at its best: hard, mild, and conditioning. The honey scent is faint at first and fades further with cure, what remains is a warm, clean bar smell.

Store cured bars on an open rack in a cool, dark cupboard. The golden colour deepens slightly over time, normal. Two years or more for a well-cured bar. Discard if orange rancid patches (DOS) appear or the bar smells sharp and paint-like.
